title: George Ross Applicant against Robert Stuart Franklin and Helen Jane Franklin Respondents And Robert Stuart Franklin and Helen Jane Franklin Applicants against George Ross Respondent [2025] SLC 8
text:
SCOTTISH LAND COURT

Citation: [2025] SLC 8,
Case reference: SLC/1/21 and SLC/36/21

OPINION OF THE COURT

Court members: Mrs Deborah Lovell,
Mr John A Smith

George Ross
Applicant
against
Robert Stuart Franklin and Helen Jane Franklin
Respondents
And
Robert Stuart Franklin and Helen Jane Franklin
Applicants
against
George Ross
Respondent

Subjects: Land at West Gruinards

The Crofters (Scotland) Act, 1993

SLC/1/21

Applicants: Ross; Inkster

Respondent: Franklin; Murchison

SLC/36/21

Applicants: Franklin; Murchison

Respondent: Ross; Inkster

7 August 2025

Introduction

[1] This decision relates to two applications in respect of the same croft, collectively known as West Gruinards in the County of Sutherland, registered with the Crofting Commission and extending in total to 316.57 ha or thereby.

The croft

[2] The croft subject to the applications comprises a number of separate and constituent areas. As a reference point we include a copy of a plan produced by Galbraith (lodged as part of the landlords’ expert’s independent report dated 13 June 2023 referred to later in this decision as “the Galbraith report”) which shows these constituent areas. This plan forms part 1A of the schedule to this decision (the “Galbraith plan”).

[3] The constituent areas are:

the croft with Crofting Commission number R2124 (C169) comprising an area of 17.4 hectares or thereby (measured by Galbraith as 18.18 hectares) shown outlined in red on the Galbraith plan;

the croft with Crofting Commission number R2125 (C170) comprising an area of 15.37 hectares or thereby (measured by Galbraith as 13.59 hectares) shown outlined in blue on the Galbraith plan; and

the croft with Crofting Commission number R2126 (C179). It should be noted here that the original application referred to this as comprising an area of 82.07 hectares or thereby and including two apportionments per the plan at schedule part 1B(3)(i) (“plan B3(i)”) which was the plan included with the crofter’s application. During the course of the application in 2022 the crofter acquired a further apportionment (in two parts) extending to 3.6 hectares as part of R2126. The crofter’s application was amended by February 2024 to make reference to this third apportionment. That apportionment is approximately the areas shown shaded red and blue on the Galbraith plan. The plan included at part 1B(3)(iii) of the schedule (“plan B3(iii)”) (which is the plan from the order on the Crofting Commission’s website) shows the extent of the third apportionment in darker blue on that plan. It can been seen more clearly from plan B3(iii) that this apportionment is in two parts (separated by another apportioned area, shaded purple, which does not pertain to this case). The Crofting Register has since been updated to the plan included as part 1B(3)(ii) of the schedule (“plan B3(ii)”) which shows the apportionment marked “Area 4” and “Area 5”. The Galbraith plan defines croft R2126 as measuring 282.57 hectares outlined in purple and the Galbraith report (at paragraph 3.1) further describes R2126 as:

“incorporating 4 areas of permanently apportioned land, which are all delineated separately on the plan, and which I understand are included in the application to purchase.”

We will refer to the darker blue shaded area on plan B3(iii) as the “western apportionment”.

[4] Within the purple outlined area on the Galbraith plan are various parts which are referred to in this decision as follows:

the areas shaded green being the original in-bye croft;

the area shaded pink comprising a previously apportioned area and what we refer to in this decision as the “northern apportionment” (and labelled as such on the plan). This is also shown on plan B3(ii) as “Area 3”; and

the area shaded purple also comprising a previously apportioned area and what we refer to in this decision as the “southern apportionment” (also labelled as such on the plan). This is also shown on plan B3(ii) as “Area 2”.

[5] We have noted the following additional point from the Galbraith report (at paragraph 3.1 supra):

“The total area of the croft land under consideration is therefore 314.34 Ha (776.73 acres). Please note the areas quoted in this section differ to those recorded in the Register of Crofts, but are based on the registered croft boundaries and are therefore considered to be more accurate than what shows on the Register of Crofts.”

We make no further comment on the area measurements. This was not raised as an issue by either party.

[6] For the purposes of this decision we will treat the crofter’s application to purchase to be in respect of the three areas shown on the plans collectively forming part 1B(1), 1B(2) and 1B(3)(ii) of the schedule to this decision (plans 1B(1) and 1B(2) of which formed the productions referred to in the original application to us). We will refer to those areas, collectively in this decision, as “the croft”.

The apportionments and the lochs

[7] The two parts of the western apportionment are adjacent to the northern apportionment (in each case, on its west). The southern apportionment is adjacent to the northern apportionment (on its south). The southern apportionment is also adjacent to a loch known as Loch a’ Bhaid-bheithe (and referred to as “Loch BB” for the purposes of this decision). Loch BB and Loch Amat can be seen on the extract part of the plan of the registered extent of the landlords’ estate (registered in the Land Register for Scotland under title number ROS10488). A section of the title plan included at schedule part 1C of the schedule to this decision (“plan 1C”) shows the extent of the landlords’ ownership (in each case shaded pink) of each loch.

The applications

[8] The first application, application SLC/1/21, was brought by the crofter, Mr Ross, to purchase his croft in terms of the provisions of section 12 of the Crofters (Scotland) Act 1993. The crofter’s application SLC/1/21 was received by the court on 5 January 2021. The application is opposed by the landlords, Mr and Mrs Franklin, under section 13(2)(b) of the 1993 Act on the basis that to grant the application would cause a substantial degree of hardship to the landlords.

[9] The second application, application SLC/36/21 was brought by the landlords, Mr and Mrs Franklin, for resumption of part of the croft under the provisions of section 20 of the 1993 Act. The resumption area is shown on a plan by Galbraith lodged as a production and forming part 1D of the schedule to this decision. The landlords’ application was received by the court on 24 March 2021. It is opposed by the crofter, Mr Ross, on the basis that the requisite tests set out in section 20 of the 1993 Act have not been met by the landlords.

[10] For the purposes of this decision we will refer to Mr Ross as the “crofter” and to Mr and Mrs Franklin as the ‘landlords’ for their respective interests in each application.

The landlords’ estate

[11] The croft forms part and portion of all and whole the lands and Estate of Gruinards, registered in the Land Register under title number ROS10488 and owned in common by the landlords. The landlords acquired the estate on 30 September 2016 (with registration on 10 October 2016).

[12] The landlords’ estate includes other crofted land held by two other crofters, namely Mr Brian Ross (Mid Gruinards, Ardgay, Sutherland) and Mr Derek Matheson (Creag Mhor, Wester Gruinards, Ardgay, Sutherland). By Order dated 12 April 2023 (SLC/90/22) the Land court authorised the landlords’ resumption of two areas of ground extending to 50.03 hectares in total or thereby, forming part of Mr Brian Ross’ croft at Mid Gruinards, under section 20 of the 1993 Act, for the purposes of forestry creation.

Procedure

[13] By order dated 27 October 2023 the court appointed both applications to be heard concurrently. It was decided that the substantive issues for both would best be resolved by hearing a full proof on both applications together.

[14] We heard evidence on 5, 6 and 7 November 2024 at a diet of proof conducted in Inverness Justice Centre. We heard submissions at Edinburgh on 26 November 2024. Mr Inkster of Inksters Solicitors appeared on behalf of the crofter. Mr Murchison of Murchison Law appeared on behalf of the landlords. The court carried out a site inspection on 16 April 2025.

[15] At the proof and in advance of witness evidence being led, the court dealt with a number of preliminary matters at the request of the parties. At the request of Mr Murchison, the court agreed to issue specific directions to all witnesses to refrain from discussing or disclosing evidence, including on social media, until conclusion of the proceedings. Further productions were lodged (including a copy of a joint minute between the experts, referred to later) and some minor referencing errors in the lists of authorities and productions were corrected. It was noted that certain productions had been lodged separately in both cases and accordingly parties would require to be clear with the referencing when directing witnesses to productions. At the request of Mr Inkster the court agreed to source and provide copies of certain past cases which had not been published.

[16] The court subsequently asked the parties for further submissions on the case of Kennedy v Smith SLC/81/15 which had not been previously cited by either party. Written submissions were received on 10 July 2025 for consideration by the court.

Authorities

[17] The parties lodged and referenced a large number of authorities. We noted that some decisions referred to by the parties in their submissions were not within the list of authorities lodged and vice versa. Some cases were cited or referred to by party but using different (from the other party and also from the version lodged) reports of the decision. For ease of reference, we have reproduced a list of authorities, including the main statutory provisions referred to in this decision, in part 2 of the schedule to this decision.

Evidence

Expert reports, joint minute and evidence

[18] In advance of the proof reports and valuations of experts appointed by each of the parties, Mr Atholl Newlands (crofter) and Ms Clare Acheson (landlords), were lodged along with a joint minute from both (referred to later). The expert evidence is critical to a number of matters in this decision. Accordingly, for ease, we have summarised the evidence presented by each expert across their reports, joint minute and evidence led at the proof in the following paragraphs.

Report of expert witness for the crofter: Mr Atholl Newlands, partner, Bowlts chartered surveyors, Member, RICS

[19] Mr Newlands was appointed on behalf of the crofter to prepare a rental assessment of crofts R2124, R2125 and R2126 and a valuation of the resumption site (as two house sites). This croft rental assessment was produced in his report dated 14 February 2024 and the house site valuations in his report dated 26 February 2024 (both lodged as productions). The basis and methodology of valuation of the croft were set out in part 9 of his report and the croft value was assessed on a market rental value of £565 per annum. The basis of valuation of the house sites was set out in part 7 of his report (being open market value of the two existing buildings and land) and each site assessed as having a value of £55,000.

Report of expert witness for the landlords: Ms Clare Acheson, partner, Galbraith, Member, RICS

[20] Ms Acheson produced the Gabraith report referred to earlier relative to her assessment of the fair rent payable in respect of the croft. In this report, Ms Acheson provided two fair rent valuations: the first based on current agricultural use only (paragraph 4 of her report) and the second being an ‘alternative purposeful use’ (paragraph 5 of her report). In doing so, she had used published data and an applied average. She had visited the croft once. She had not seen any farm accounts. Her value of the fair rent assessed on an agricultural basis was £2,238 per annum and assessed on an alternative purposeful use basis was £3,881.23 per annum.

Joint minute of the experts

[21] As ordained by the court, Mr Newlands and Ms Acheson met to prepare a joint minute setting out points of agreement and disagreement, to be read alongside their reports. That joint minute, dated 30 August 2024, set out the position of each expert under the following headings:

Purchase application: (1) (i) “Fair rent for West Gruinards Croft – agricultural basis” and (ii) “Fair Rent – Consideration of alternative purposeful use”; and (2) “Valuation of Reserved Timber”; and

Application to resume: (1) “Valuation of buildings for resumption on basis that redevelopment is within permitted development. Valuation with and without planning permission”; and (2) “Requirements (including access and duration) and likely cost of surveys related to birds, bats etc”.

Joint minute: Purchase application

[22] In respect of the “fair rent – agricultural basis” the experts agreed to follow the methodology set out in Ms Acheson’s report. They agreed that the stocking level for the croft should be 210 ewes but after that they applied differing calculations to come to their individual conclusions. Ms Acheson’s assessed rent was £2,143.82 while Mr Newlands’ was £1,530.22.The valuation of reserved timber was agreed at £8,500.

[23] On the “fair rent – alternative purposeful use basis” the experts were not agreed with the approach. Mr Newlands was not instructed to deal with the question of the hypothetical tenant and has never seen this test before. His concerns around the use of this approach had been raised and discussed with Ms Acheson at the meeting to agree the joint minute and were recorded as comments in the joint minute.

Joint minute: Resumption application

[24] In respect of the valuation of the buildings for resumption the assessment of the experts in the joint minute was:

“The market value of the buildings without planning permission is likely to be c.£25,000-£30,000 per site. The market value of the buildings with planning permission in place might be £55,000-£60,000 per site.”

Evidence of experts at the hearing

[25] The court heard from both experts on the second day of the evidential hearing. The court agreed to allow the evidence of Ms Acheson to be heard ‘out of order’ in order to accommodate a prior commitment on her part. Ms Acheson’s evidence was therefore heard before that of Mr Newlands as expert witness for the crofter. In the course of Mr Newlands giving evidence it was noted by the landlords’ agent that it was not possible for certain comments and concerns raised by Mr Newlands on the proposed “fair rent – alternative purposeful use basis” to be put to Ms Acheson, Ms Acheson already having been discharged as a witness by that time. Given that Mr Newlands had not been instructed to deal with such methodology but, by his own evidence, had expressed his concerns at the meeting of the experts (which concerns were summarised in the joint minute), it is our view that Ms Acheson had had fair notice of the points of concern ahead of her appearance. She was given the opportunity to respond to and comment on such. Accordingly the court does not consider that this has had any bearing on the decision reached as set out below.

Ms Acheson

Purchase application

[26] With regard to the agricultural use fair rent valuation, she and Mr Newlands were agreed on the amount attributable to the sheep margin but not on the subsidies. There was a question between them over whether the fair rent should be based on current or future rent. As the levels 2 years away are not known and the position is speculative a 30% discount had been applied.

[27] The alternative purposeful use approach was not an agreed position with Mr Newlands and she had not used this method of valuation before. It has not been done on this basis before to her knowledge. She had undertaken a desktop survey only. She was proposing a combined use for planting or forestry (native woodland rather than commercial) and agriculture. She had rejected tourism as a prospective use on the basis of the capital outlay required and the lack of demand.

[28] She acknowledged that there were risks with the approach. Unless carbon units were sold (after year 5), it would take 6 years to get to a profit basis. A party doing this would, therefore, need some way to finance themselves until then. There are risks to selling units. A unit can only be sold once and only when it is validated. The main risks for a landowner is that they may have no valid claim for any subsidy (which needs to come from an accredited scheme) and there is a liability to the party to whom the unit is sold if the expected value is not delivered. Presently there are two more years guaranteed at the current rates. The impact on rents is unclear: this is a capital income stream and involves a degree of long‑term commitment.

[29] She was not aware of the proposed windfarm development on the common grazing. She acknowledged this may impact on her proposal with potential issues around the planting of trees affecting any proposed development. On the other hand, the developer may carry out a compensatory planting scheme as part of the development and that could deliver benefit to the croft. She agreed that there is usually an exclusion zone but that native woodland is likely to be less disruptive than commercial.

Resumption application

[30] Valuation ranges were given in the joint minute for the buildings with and without planning permission. The valuation with the benefit of planning is higher as it reflects additional time and costs to get planning due to the presence of wildlife. She was not aware of the Franklins’ proposals to demolish the existing buildings and rebuild these for use as holiday lets. In her view there was a lack of demand for such use. The capital expenditure involved was unlikely to be readily recovered through the likely levels of holiday rental income.

Mr Newlands

Purchase application

[31] He has concerns around the “alternative purposeful use” test advanced by the landlords and set out in the Galbraith report. He has never seen the “alternative purposeful use” test used before. He accepts that Ms Acheson’s approach is reasonable and balanced and he has no issues with her methodology or assumptions nor any reason to doubt her desktop analysis or integrity. However in his view there are a number of costs, risks and limitations associated with proposed scheme as set out that means it is not viable.

[32] In his view the scheme would not be viable without addressing fundamental issues in the approach. The first is that an application for any woodland creation scheme must be made and approved. Surveys will then determine the suitability for such a scheme. There are then significant start up costs to implement the scheme and risks associated with it once built. The second issue is that the approach relies on an income stream from carbon credits which carry inherent risks in actual realisation and the current rates for which are only guaranteed for another 2 years. As a tenant crofter cannot get the carbon without the landlords consent, both the landlords and the tenant need to sign up. It was not clear that the scheme binds successors, even where the crofter is the owner rather than tenant. Ms Acheson’s indicative scheme showed that it could take up to 6 years to get to a profit basis. A party doing this would, therefore, need some way to fina.nce themselves until then. In Mr Newland’s view, the risks with the approach are so high, no hypothetical tenant would take them.

Resumption application

[33] He was not previously aware of the landlords’ proposed demolition and rebuild of the two derelict buildings for use as holiday lets. He had discounted tourism as a viable purposeful use by a crofter in his report and confirmed the same comments would apply to the landlords’ proposals. He and Ms Acheson are in agreement in discounting tourism as a viable use though he did accept that he has no direct experience in what he referred to as a difficult area.

Other witness evidence

[34] In advance of the hearing, witness statements and productions were lodged by each of the parties. As the two applications were being heard concurrently, all witnesses gave evidence on relevant matters for both applications. Each witness adopted their statements and spoke to those statements and the productions, all of which had been lodged into process. As the application to purchase was received first, the crofter led their witness evidence first (other than the evidence of Ms Acheson, taken out of turn, as referred to above). We do not attempt to summarise all the evidence given by witnesses or established by the documentary productions. Although all evidence led has been considered thoroughly we will set out the main issues of fact upon which our decision is based and, where appropriate, make reference to the evidence bearing on these issues.

[35] We took note of the fact that Dr Ross’ witness statements (presented as an affidavit and then supplementary witness statement), in each case, states that she has read the witness statement and supplementary witness statement of her husband, the crofter and “can confirm and agree with everything stated in that Witness Statement”. Neither statement set relevant matters out in her own words. Each of Mr and Mrs Franklin’s supplementary witness statements also, in part, made reference to agreeing with or endorsing the other’s supplementary statement. Such statements are not statements made in the witnesses own words setting out their personal knowledge and observations. In each case we therefore gave weight to the direct evidence heard from each witness over such statements. While Dr Ross is not a party to the application and should have provided her own statement, we do not consider this impacted on Dr Ross’s credibility.

[36] As a general observation, we found all witnesses to be credible and reliable in their accounts. It was evident that the crofter and the landlords held differing views on several key matters, and the tone of prior communications and the overall dispute has obviously at times been acrimonious. However, even where we preferred one account over another, we did not consider differences in any account to be the result of any dishonesty on the part of any witness. Rather, they appeared to reflect genuine divergences in perspective, shaped by each party’s individual experiences and understanding. Where possible, we assessed their positions against independent evidence. Having been appointed by the court to confer on certain relevant issues, we gave the opinions of the expert witnesses appropriate and considered weight. For the present purposes, we simply give an indication of the broad scope of the evidence given by each witness in the following paragraphs.

Witnesses led for the crofter

Mr George Adam Ross

[37] There is a long family history on the croft: his father and grandfather previously had stewardship of the croft before his father transferred the tenancies to him in 2015. His forbearers built the buildings on the land subject to the resumption application which are iconic and have meaning for and a place in crofting history.

[38] His approach is to farm the croft for sheep on a sustainable basis. He has particular regard and concern for wildlife and biodiversity seeing these as extremely important to the future sustainability of the croft. His existing seasonal grazings let had not been renewed by the landlords, resulting in the sale of some of his flock. As a result he had looked into other uses, including for the tourism tours, primarily managed by his wife, and which take in the buildings as part of the historical background of the croft.

Purchase application

[39] His father had previously attempted to buy the croft. He, himself, had first made an approach to the previous estate owners in 2016 to negotiate a purchase. The estate had then been sold to the landlords. He resumed his request to agree terms for a purchase with the landlords in 2017. Negotiations did not progress to any agreement and in November 2020 the landlords wrote to advise that they wished to resume part of the croft.

[40] He had interactions with the landlords on various applications for apportionments, the formation of a crofting committee and the proposals for the prospective windfarm scheme at the estate. Previously the three crofters have objected to plans for the common grazings as two of them had put proposals for forestry planting on this area in to the landlords.

[41] He has publicly voiced opposition to the windfarm scheme but is now more open minded and educated on windfarms and is prepared to consider a detailed proposal. In particular he is willing to engage on the placement of turbines including having a discussion about an 11th turbine on the southern apportionment. He had contacted the developer to ensure that the developer understood his croft holding and plans to buy. He has concerns about the way his land has been shown in plans produced to date. His view is that there is no difference in the windfarm development being delivered whether he is a tenant or an owner: he already has the right to plant trees and erect structures without landlords’ consent.

[42] He has no general intention to develop the land should he buy the croft, whether for housing or forestry. He presently uses the buildings on the resumption site for storage and the sheep use it for shelter. He has parked his ATVs behind the buildings to shield them from the public road. He accepts that the buildings are dilapidated and storm damaged. He previously obtained a quotation for works at a cost of £19,800 to address this. He now has longer term plans for the two buildings himself: to renovate one to a state suitable for storage and to renovate the other for a local family to occupy, ideally one who would work on the croft. Providing a family home will be a better way to support crofting life and address affordable housing shortages than the landlords’ plans. His plans will also be less disruptive as he will carry out works on one building at a time and preserve the wildlife in his conversion plans. As his plans involve significant spend, he has received advice not to do works until he owns the land.

Resumption application

[43] He has a number of concerns with the landlords’ plans. The proposed works will disrupt wildlife, including existing scrapes for waders and resident nesting barn owls. This could affect his existing Agri-Environment Climate Scheme contract which requires the promotion of biodiversity practices on the croft. Issues will arise from the increase in visitors to the croft, particularly if visitors bring dogs. He accepts that the tour groups involve visitors to the croft but the groups are managed by them and they do not bring dogs. He accepted that initial concerns he had over a possible impact on the water supply for the landlords’ proposed development from his practice of spreading manure in the vicinity of the two buildings are misplaced.

[44] He is concerned that the landlords will resume the site but then do nothing with it. He is wary of the landlords from previous experience with them, in particular following the previous resumption of croft land for forestry. He had understood this was for the purposes of native planting rather than the commercial forestry use actually made by the landlords. He accepts that this went through the proper channels but sees it as a loss of good crofting land. In the context of the need for greater food security the resumption of 50 acres of good croft land does not make sense to him. The landlords have planted trees on ploughable land.

[45] He can see the advantages of using the compensation from the resumption for a new agriculture shed but this does not outweigh the non-monetary disadvantages of losing the land and buildings. His preference is to retain the existing buildings and utilise these: this would minimise any adverse effects on the wildlife and preserve the buildings, respecting their historical significance.

[46] The southern apportionment and Loch BB are not used by the landlords. His sheep use the southern apportionment, especially in the summer months overnight. The gates are left open. The access route saves the peat bog from being damaged. There are protected and threatened wildlife using the area. The presence of deer on the southern apportionment is an overflow of the deer which are over-grazing the common grazings. That affects his use of the area as part of his croft.

Dr Sabrina Ross

[47] Dr Ross, 41, is Mr Ross’s wife and a trained veterinary surgeon, currently working as an agricultural officer for the Scottish Government. She has lived and worked on the croft since 2012. Her attitude to the landlord’s proposed windfarm development is that this is speculative. Generally she would prefer windfarms to be offshore. She would not for example want a turbine located on peat land. She was not invited to the meeting among the developer, landlords and crofters in January 2023 and has not seen an option plan. She would need to see the proposals to be able to provide her views on the proposals. The two resumption buildings are used for storage, wildlife and shelter. Their commercial vehicles are parked behind the building to shield these from the road and possible theft. The land next to the buildings is also used as a fank. Their proposals for future use of the buildings is to renovate one building for use by a family with the other building retained for use by barn owls. They first asked to buy the croft in 2016/17 and obtained an estimate for works before the resumption application was made. Advice given to them has been not to spend until they own the buildings and any plans have therefore been put on hold while the court case is running.

[48] The recent tourism activity on the croft has been to supplement income lost after common grazing land was lost. They have a holiday pod on their private land and she has a wool business. The tours started this year and they have had two so far with others booked. They are run by a third party and their croft forms a stop on a wider tour of Scotland. Visitors view the wool business and the ruined buildings on the croft and hear about the importance of these buildings to the historical background of the croft. The croft is historically important and is referenced in books. The buildings are an integral part of the croft and that is gone if these are demolished.

[49] She has concerns around risks to wildlife, security and biodiversity and biosecurity if the land is resumed for the landlords’ proposed use and visitors to the croft increase as a result. The croft is a special place and includes peat bogs which are important for the carbon audit. She is concerned about the loss of crofting land and that hardship that will be caused to them from the loss of the buildings.

[50] She is not familiar with the landlords’ use of Loch BB but does accept that she would would not see this from the house. She is not aware of the landlords being on the Estate too frequently. She can say that the boat located on the side of Loch BB has been moved recently in a way that blocks sheep and a fence at the southern apportionment was broken in the last couple of weeks.

Mr James McGillivray

[51] Mr McGillivray, 72, was formerly Chairman of the Kyle of Sutherland Branch of the Crofters Union until taking up his current position as an independent Highland Councilor. Mr McGillivray and his father had known Mr Ross’s father and how he worked the croft. Mr McGillivray had been Mr Ross’s teacher and considered him skilled as a crofter.

[52] His view is that the landlords’ proposals to resume the land and redevelop the existing buildings for holiday accommodation are unusual and not something he has come across before. He does not consider the location of the old croft houses to be suitable for holiday accommodation as the land is boggy and there is no view. He was unaware that the experts have said planning would succeed. The buildings had been built by Mr Ross’s father and were an intrinsic and important part of the croft in his view. They are better used for croft purposes. Demolition of the buildings would result in a loss of culture.

[53] On a visit to the croft the previous autumn he observed the buildings being used for storage. He had entered the buildings. He took no precautions in doing so as the buildings seemed structurally sound. He considered them not to be watertight but serviceable. He thought they needed some work to make useful as part of the croft for storage. If the concerns of the landlords were that the buildings were in poor repair then they should offer to assist in the repairs.

[54] He understands that modern buildings are better than renovated old buildings but the crofter would need to get planning consents and construct the new buildings before the resumption occurred.

[55] There has been strong community objections to the proposed windfarm development. It may be of benefit to the landlords but there were concerns about any benefit to the crofter. He is aware that there is a community benefit proposed in the form of an electric charger but this seems insignificant. He sees this as a balance between development going ahead and communities accessing funding. He was not able to answer whether there would be any different impact on windfarm development arising from the sale when compared to the right of a crofter to grow trees and build buildings.

Mr Robert Lockhart Swann

[56] Mr Swann, 73, is a local ornithological expert, local organiser for the British Trust for Ornithology and primary bird surveyor for North of Scotland Ornithological Services, conducting bird surveys throughout the Highlands on both a voluntary and professional basis, including for developers. He is a licensed bird ringer. He was formerly a teacher and taught Mr Ross. He knows the croft well and has maintained bird boxes and carried out bird ringing on the croft (last done prior to covid time and not since). He was consulted by Mr Ross in 2023 about the landlords’ proposals to convert (as the proposals were at that time) the buildings for holiday accommodation and the likely effect on resident nesting and breeding barn owls. He provided Mr Ross with a note of his comments on 18 July 2023, an extract from which formed part of his witness statement.

[57] He is aware of the landlords’ proposals and has concerns around the likely impact that demolition of the buildings will have on the birds and on the wider local owl population more generally. His experience of likely planning wildlife mitigation measures were that they were often unsuccessful as they tended to remove or relocate the birds from their territory. Other animals such as pinemartins would compete for the nesting boxes often used in the relocations. The best mitigation measures would be to replace the birds existing nest with a new internal box in the building and time development works around breeding times, in line with legal requirements (it being a criminal offence to disturb breeding birds). Submissions

[79] The court received very detailed notes of argument and written submissions from each of the parties in advance of the hearing on 5, 6 and 7 November 2024. The parties respectively adopted these positions in the hearing. The position of each of the parties in respect of each application is summarised in the following paragraphs. In each case the court was invited by each of the parties to find a considerable number of facts as set out in the submissions to be proven. Given that considerable number, we see no merit in listing each fact and instead have referred to what we consider to be the relevant facts supported by the evidence led in our discussion below.

Application to purchase - arguments led for the crofter

[80] On the basis of the court finding the (73) facts as stated, the landlords are not able to demonstrate the requirements of section 13(2) of the 1993 Act, namely either or both a substantial degree of hardship would be caused to the landlords or it would be substantially detrimental to the interests of sound management of the landlords’ estate if the application was granted.

[81] The landlords put forward the position that substantial hardship will be caused to the landlords in two core ways should the crofter’s application be granted, namely: (1) material risk to a proposed windfarm development proceeding and (2) loss of access to or use of the western side of the landlords’ estate, in particular Loch BB. Submissions in respect of the first issue (the windfarm development) were only introduced by the landlords and were introduced by them at a later stage (16 June 2023) than the original application (30 March 2021).

[82] The hardship to the landlord or detriment to the estate requires to be of a substantial nature for any objection to succeed (Mackay v Trustees of Miss S N Barr 1981 SLCR App 76 and Geddes v Martin 1987 SLCR 104). The test is a high test (Waugh v Thrumster Estate Limited (Brickigoe) (Application RN SLC/156/05 – 18 August 2006)). Cases cannot be decided on speculation but on the evidence led and submissions made (Rodenhurst v Thrumster Estate Limited (Application RN SLC/26/11 – 17 July 2015 referred to).

[83] In response to a suggestion by the landlords that, in establishing hardship, the court is to have regard to the proportion of the land to be purchased as it bears to the size of the estate (the higher the proportion, the greater the risk of hardship), the cases of Geddes v Martin (supra) and Rodenhurst v Thrumster Estate Limited (supra) are relevant. Geddes can be distinguished as here, proportionately, the croft to be acquired compared to the estate is much smaller than in Geddes. In any event, the landlords have led no evidence of any significant attempt at management that would be affected should the application be granted (Rodenhurst v Thrumster Estate Limited (supra)).

First core way: windfarm development

[84] Any information presented to the court has been sketchy at best. No heads of terms were produced to the court and the exclusivity agreement produced incorrectly defines the crofter’s apportionments as being part of the common grazing. The draft option agreement produced excludes the apportionments from the option site. Any current plans to develop a windfarm are in respect of 10 turbines on the common grazing and not on the apportionments, in particular the southern apportionment.

[85] No evidence has been led by the landlords, the windfarm developer or any independent windfarm developer of any impact on the proposed development by the grant of the crofter’s application. No evidence has been led by the landlords that the landlords would have any greater degree of control over activities on the crofter’s land that might affect the proposed development if the application was refused than they would have should it be granted. Indeed evidence to the contrary has been led. When making a determination of whether a landlord would be caused a substantial degree of hardship, a comparison of the positions with or without the order is required (Fraser v MacKintosh 1995 SLCR 91 and Waugh v Thrumster Estate Ltd (South Yarrows) Application RN SLC/157/05 – 18 August 2006).

[86] No detailed financial breakdown has been provided by the landlords as to any financial hardship that might occur. At most, the hardship would equate to a speculative 50% of the rental income of one turbine that may possibly be located on the southern apportionment. If the application was granted it would not preclude the developer seeking the consent of the crofter to an 11th turbine on the southern apportionment. The landlords would benefit from 50% of the rental income during the subsisting 10 year clawback security period, part of any acquisition order.

[87] The onus is on the landlords to present evidence to support their case (Macaskill v Basil Baird & Sons Ltd and Another 1986 SLCR 133). The cases of MacDonald v Hilleary 1992 SLCR 51, Mackay v Trustees of Miss S N Barr 1981 (supra), Geddes v Martin (supra), Rodenhurst v Thrumster Estate Limited (supra), Fraser v MacKintosh (supra) and Waugh v Thrumster Estate Ltd (South Yarrows) (supra) are all authority that, when applied to the found facts, the landlords have not met the high test required.

[88] Macaskill v Basil Baird & Sons Limited and Another (supra) and MacDonald v Hilleary (supra) are cases where not enough detail was presented to allow the court to make a decision based on hardship or detriment to sound estate management. This is the case here. On the contrary evidence points to there being no such hardship or detriment to sound estate management.

[89] Instead of being able to decide based on evidence led and submissions made, the court has been invited by the landlords to consider what might happen with a windfarm development on the estate on an anticipated or speculative basis. Any comparison of the position of the landlords with or without the order being granted would essentially show no difference. If anything it would show the landlords in a better position with the order granted given the sale price receipt.

Second core way – Loch BB

[90] On the second core way, namely access to and use of the western side of the estate, in particular Loch BB, no evidence was led relative to the western side. The only issue of real concern would appear to be access to and use of Loch BB. Loch BB is not used by the landlords for estate purposes but rather for private leisure purposes only. The loss of Loch BB would not impact financially but emotionally. Waugh v Thrumster Estate Ltd (South Yarrows) 2006 SLCR (2) 53 considered emotional hardship and concluded that, as the party in that case was a limited company, it was not capable of suffering emotional hardship. However the court had not been referred to Mackenzie v Hardy and Another 1998 SLCR 49 which dealt with emotional hardship.

[91] The loss of Loch BB does not provide anywhere near the degree of hardship necessary to warrant refusal of the application. There is a question of whether emotional hardship can be established on the basis of the comparison test in Fraser v MacKintosh. Following the reasoning in Waugh v Thrumster Estate Ltd (South Yarrows) (supra) it is irrelevant that the business is not held in the name of a limited company given that the estate is owned by the landlords as a business. Granting the application will not deprive the landlords of the right to access and use Loch BB as they will have the right to roam for recreational purposes. A sporting lease will be granted for a right to fish for trout for 21 years: this despite the fact that they have never fished for estate purposes.

Inclusion of lochs in application

[92] The landlords’ position is that, as the two lochs are not included in the Crofting Register they cannot form part of the purchase application. This ignores the law relating to ownership of lochs as set out in Rankine, Reid, Gloag & Henderson, Robbie, Gordon and Stair, which textbooks refer to a number of relevant case authorities to support their stated propositions. The result is that if the application is granted, the lochs in so far as bounded by the croft will be included as a pertinent of the grant.

[93] It would be anomalous to exclude the lochs and leave these in estate ownership lying within owner/occupied crofts. It would also negate the need for sporting leases for trout fishing which exist for the reason that lochs and rivers will pass into the ownership of crofters exercising their rights to buy when these crofts have lochs or rivers on their boundaries. On the estate when Derek Matheson purchased his croft the adjacent river was not excluded from his title and a sporting lease was granted for brown trout fishing for 21 years.

Southern apportionment

[94] The landlords have suggested that the southern apportionment is not contiguous or adjacent to the croft and therefore should be excluded from the crofter’s acquisition. The meaning of “adjacent or contiguous” was considered by the case of Gillies v Countess of Sutherland’s Trs 1978 SLT (Land Ct) 2 and Ross v Trustees of Miss S N Barr 1994 SLCR 60 at 71. All apportionments including the southern apportionment are contiguous or adjacent to any other part of the croft. The crofts and apportionments together form one complete unit with no separation between them.

[95] The landlords have suggested that the southern apportionment is not used by the crofter and, to the extent that it is used, it is not worked in conjunction with his croft. It is grazed throughout the year and used overnight by sheep in the summer. The sheep are free to roam as the crofter is managing the croft for the benefit of biodiversity, namely breeding waders.

Area also subject to application to resume

[96] This should be included with the acquisition and the resumption refused for the reasons submitted in that application. Concerns of the landlords around the condition of the buildings on the area will vanish once the crofter has bought (Bowman v Guthrie 1997 SLCR 40).

Terms and conditions of purchase

[97] The terms and conditions of the purchase, including the consideration payable to the landlords are to be determined by the court in terms of section 13 and section 14 of the 1993 Act. In granting the application the court should consider imposing terms and conditions as set out, namely: the purchase to be subject to the existing 175 year shooting lease and a new 21 year brown trout fishing lease in Loch BB at £1 per annum granted; mineral rights reserved and a clawback security granted in the usual way; rent for the deemed croft (grazing rights in the common grazings) fixed by the court; no servitudes reserved for estate purposes; crofter to produce the title plan; and mutual fences to be mutually maintained. Reserved timber should be valued at the agreed valuation of £8,500. Any access rights required by the landlords would be granted in the sporting lease and not reserved in the conveyance.

[98] The experts for each party have proposed adjusted fair rents in terms of their joint minute and evidence. The landlords have suggested that the fair rent should be higher, taking into account a hypothetical tenant carrying out a forestry scheme on the croft. There is no basis for assessment in this manner. It is also not supported by the landlords’ position that it does not wish any forestry on the croft in case that affects the proposed windfarm development. It should be assessed in line with Borland v Crofters on the Lochend Estate (Applications RN SLC/137/17, SLC/138/17, SLC/139/17, SLC/140/17 – 7 June 2019) and fixed by the court in terms of section 14(2) of the 1993 Act.

[99] The landlord’s view is that, if the court does not agree, in any event the assessed rent should be no greater than the landlords’ expert and no lower than the crofter’s expert values is not sound. These are to assist the court but the court is the expert and should fix the rent. The only minimum figure the court requires to consider is the minimum level of £30 (Anderton v Crofters having rights in crofts on the Vaila Estate (Application RN SLC/68/22 – 6 February 2024)).

[100] A timetable should be laid down by the court for the grant of conveyancing and associated deeds to avoid any delay (such as was experienced in Rodenhurst v Thrumster Estate Limited (supra) .

[101] Expenses should be reserved pending the court’s decision.

Application to purchase - arguments led by the landlords

[102] There will be substantial hardship to the landlords if the order is granted, arising from two consequences. The first is to risk a proposed windfarm development situated primarily on the common grazing but with a possible turbine requirement on the croft (on the southern apportionment) from either going ahead only on a restricted basis or not going ahead at all. The second is the restriction of access to and use of retained land on the western side of the landlords’ estate, in particular Loch BB. Substantial hardship need not be financial: it can be emotional.

Windfarm development

[103] The crofter’s sole ground of opposition to the landlords’ position is that there can be no substantial hardship because the windfarm development is merely speculative. That was not supported by the evidence. An exclusivity agreement has been entered into and a first draft option and lease provided to the landlords. The extent of the area covered by the exclusivity agreement (which includes both crofter’s apportionments and designated wild land) is entirely understandable when the requirement for wind protection zones and restrictions on development within the vicinity of the turbines is factored in. A site inspection of the topography would assist the court in understanding why the exclusivity agreement covers the area it does.

[104] There is a constraint on the number of turbines within the common grazing due to the designated wild land. It is possible that a 10 turbine development may not be feasible but an 11 turbine development will be. Even in a 10 turbine development the wind protection zone and non-development areas will include the land the crofter seeks to purchase. The income to the estate of the proposed development is likely to be at least £16 million over the 37 year period of the lease.

[105] The estate when acquired by the landlords was in a run-down condition. It is still running at a loss. There is a stark contrast between the income of the estate without the development and the income of the estate should it go ahead. That increased income stream would benefit the crofters on the estate. The crofter has demonstrated opposition to any windfarm development and therefore there is no basis for concluding that he will co-operate in progressing a windfarm should he acquire ownership of the croft. If the crofter’s application succeeds there is a real danger to the progress of a windfarm development. The landlords’ evidence on this point should be preferred as being credible and reliable when compared to the crofter. The crofter’s position that the windfarm development is merely speculative cannot be sustained.

[106] If the court considers that there is a degree of contingency or uncertainty in the evidence as to the effect of making the order then the court should consider that ‘substantial hardship’ can be contrasted conceptually with an insubstantial degree of hardship. The policy of the 1993 Act appears intended to exclude minor or trivial hardship only. The factors on which the court heard evidence including the sums involved in achieving planning, the constrained area for development and the crofter’s hostile (or at best unpredictable) attitude to the development means that a finding of substantial hardship is appropriate even if viewed as a loss of opportunity.

[107] Loss of opportunity is a recognised form of loss (Kyle v P & J Stormonth Darling WS 1992 SC 57). English law recognises this as real loss within the law of damages (Chaplin v Hicks 1911 2 KB 786). The crofter would have to satisfy the court that there is only a very small chance the opportunity to progress the windfarm would be lost in order to say there would be no hardship caused. In the absence of that there is the degree of materiality that brings the case within the realm of a substantial degree of hardship.

Southern apportionment

[108] The landlords do not seek to advance any argument that substantial detriment will be caused by being unable to enforce the duty of cultivation (Malone v Pattinson (Application RN SLC/39/17 – 10 October 2018). Rather the southern apportionment should be excluded on the basis that this area is not sufficiently adjacent or contiguous to any other part of the croft. The cases of Gillies v Countess of Sutherland Trs (supra) and Ross v Trustees of Miss N Barr (supra) are specifically referred to in respect of the principles of adjacency.

[109] The evidence of Mr Oxley was that he has never seen stock on the southern apportionment. The crofter concedes that, to the extent he uses it at all, it is used differently from other parts of the croft. Some of the photos lodged in evidence were taken after Mr Oxley’s statement. To the extent it is worked at all, it is not worked in the same way as the rest of the croft.

Use of Loch BB

[110] The Franklins gave evidence of their use of and access to Loch BB and its importance to their family and enjoyment of the estate. If the purchase were to proceed then they have justifiable concerns from the past actions of the crofter that they would be prevented from accessing Loch BB in the future.

[111] In the event that the court was minded to make the purchase order then this should be subject to such terms and conditions as the court thinks appropriate in terms of section 13 of the 1993 Act having regard to the location and layout of the croft and also existing title conditions (as the same are defined in section 122 of the Title Conditions (Scotland) Act 2003).

[112] Mineral rights are reserved in terms of section 13(1)(a) of the 1993 Act. The landlords should have all appropriate ancillary rights consistent with Anderson v Williamson 1997 SLCR 23. The landlords and those authorised by them should have the right to mine including a right to enter the surface.

[113] The value of the reserved timber is agreed at £8,500. There should be a 10 year claw back security under sections 13(4) and 14(3) of the 1993 Act. Rent for the deemed croft consisting of grazing rights in the common grazing should be set by the court.

[114] The areas subject to the landlords’ application to resume should be excluded (referencing the court’s comments in Davie v The Trustees of the Countess of Sutherland’s No.3 Settlement SLC 2005 SLCR 137 at p162). Servitudes should be granted for drainage, water, electricity and services required for normal estate management or in connection with the resumed land. Mutual fences should be mutually maintained per the approach in Grant v Countess of Seafield’s Trs 1979 SLT (Land Ct) 7 and Nevis Estates Ltd v Cameron 2011 SLCR 117. The crofter should produce the title plan.

[115] Unhindered rights of access for current estate business and any future business reasonably in contemplation, including access for sporting rights, access to Loch BB and Loch Amat (which otherwise would be landlocked in each case) and access to and service rights for buildings and sites subject of the landlords’ application to resume should be granted (Inverness Seafield Development Co Ltd v Mackintosh 2001 SC 406 at [13] and [14]).

[116] Pedestrian and vehicle access to the area for the purposes of allowing the developer to exercise rights contained in the exclusivity agreement should be granted. The estate should have all rights to allow for the development of a windfarm project. Not all rights re capable of being created as title conditions which is why the purchase order should be refused: title conditions alone will not meet a developer’s requirements. However, certain specific title conditions should be created in order to prevent competing or restricting development or activity. The parties will agree the precise wording, which failing the court should.

[117] The price should be determined under section 14(2) of the 1993 Act. Certain reserved rights in terms sufficient to support potential windfarm development and for any area resumed under the landlords’ application to resume should be granted.

[118] The landlords wish to make clear within the context of the right to buy application they have an esto plea in law that if [not [sic]] granted then the rent should be reviewed (Lawson v Lord Strathcona 1992 SLCR 67 and Agnew: Crofting Law at p85).

Application for resumption - arguments for landlords

[119] Acknowledging that the “reasonable purpose” test has regard to the good of the croft, the good of the estate, the public interest and the good of the crofting community, many and varied purposes have previously been determined as reasonable by the court. The landlords’ proposed redevelopment of the two ruinous buildings on the area subject of the application is a reasonable purpose in satisfaction of the test under section 20 of the 1993 Act.

[120] There is a weighing of factors to be undertaken. The court is permitted to take account of the factors identified at sections 20(1AA) and 20(1AC) of the 1993 Act when assessing the public interest test. While it is anticipated that the crofter will raise concerns over the presence of wildlife as falling with the factor identified within section 20(1AC)(a)(iv) of the 1993 Act, the joint position taken by the parties’ respective experts is both that planning permission for redevelopment would be granted and any planning permission would include measures to be taken for the appropriate protection of statutorily protected species.

[121] There are a number of factors supporting the resumption being for a reasonable purpose, including that the area to be resumed is modest, the landlords’ intended redevelopment for affordable holiday accommodation would provide employment, income for the estate and economic activity for the wider community and provide a solution to the dangers and risks posed by the ruinous state of the current buildings on the area to be resumed. Such redevelopment cannot take place until this area is resumed as proposed.

[122] The concerns of the crofter raised in regard to environmental and wildlife protection matters apply alike for his stated intended use of the buildings. The crofter has however provided no detailed proposals or information on any wildlife mitigation measures or works required. It is appropriate for the court to apply the same standard to both proposals when assessing reasonable purpose. It would be unusual for the court to reject the landlords’ proposal in comparison with the tentative or speculative proposal of the crofter. The quote for works produced by the crofter do not correspond with his stated intentions. A failure to address the state and condition of the buildings would not support the tour business proposal of the crofter. The objections put forward by the crofter to the landlords’ proposals relate more to matters for the assessment of the planning authority rather than to relevant considerations on whether or not the purpose is reasonable.

[123] An argument has been made by the crofter that the resumption should not be granted as no planning consent has been granted for the landlords’ proposed development. The experts have agreed that planning permission would be granted for the landlords’ proposed scheme of development and that such planning permission would include all necessary mitigation measures. The experts appointed by each of the landlords and crofter have jointly agreed that planning will be granted for the landlords’ proposal.

[124] Reliance is made on Practice Note (No. 1) Resumption Application of the court (“Practice Note 1”)). The current situation can be distinguished such that Practice Note 1 does not apply: in this case there is no intention to erect houses on bare land. Even if the court was to disagree with this, Lands Improvements Holdings Landmatch SARL v Cole (supra) is authority for the case that the practice note should not be treated as creating a rule in addition to the legislation. If the court holds that planning permission would be a requirement for any resumption then the application could be continued to allow this to be obtained. Rule 16 and Rule 1(1) [of The Rules of the Scottish Land Court Order 2014, SSI 2014 No 229] would permit this course of action. Indeed this would be an appropriate way to proceed where the obtaining of planning permission would incur significant costs and there is opposition from the crofter to any redevelopment taking place. To decide otherwise would mean every landlord would require to expend time and money with no guarantee the resumption would be granted.

[125] Compensation should be determined in terms of sections 20 and 21 of the 1993 Act. Section 21(2) provides that the share payable by the crofter is half the difference between the open market value and the crofting value. The crofting value will be the proportion of the current passing rent attributable to the resumed area multiplied by 15. The experts appointed by each of the landlords and crofter have agreed a valuation of £55,000 to £60,000 per site. The landlords are agreeable to a mid range valuation of £57,500 as representing the open market value. The landlords are prepared to concede that the likely apportioned crofting value is so negligible as to apply a nil value.

Application for resumption - arguments led by the crofter

[126] The landlords are seeking resumption of buildings which form part of the croft, are crofter’s improvements and are used by the crofter as an integral part of the croft. Specifically, they are used for storage, stock shelter, quad bike security and as a nature habitat for wildlife including two breeding barn owls. Such resumption is for the purpose of conversion to holiday lets. This is not a reasonable purpose having relation to the statutory test, namely having relation to the good of the croft, or of the estate or to the public interest or to the interests of the crofting community in the locality of the croft.

[127] The application was made only in response to the crofter’s application to purchase. The application is premature in any event as planning permission has not been applied for or granted. It is therefore contrary to Practice Note 1 of the court. The landlords’ invitation to the court to make any resumption order subject to planning within 6 months is at odds with the practice of granting resumption orders and with the crofter’s application to purchase.

[128] In considering the relevant tests, the fact the purpose for which a landlord seeks to resume the land is one of those referred to does not ipso facto mean that it is a reasonable purpose in all the circumstances requiring the application to be granted automatically (Mackay’s Trs v Colthart 1959 SLCR 43). Even where ex facie reasonable the landlord must lead evidence to meet any objections to the application (Clegg v MacPherson 1963 SLCR App 108; Secretary for State for Air v Macdonald 1962 SLCR App 30; Countess of Sutherland v Shareholder in Doll Common Grazings 1970 SLCR App 85; South Uist Estates Ltd v MacDonald 1983 SLCR 86). The crofter has set out many valid objections: the landlords have failed to lead evidence to meet these.

[129] The crofter’s plan is to repair and improve the buildings. This is long standing, well thought out and costed and predates the landlords’ interest in them. The landlords in contrast have not applied for planning permission nor costed their proposed development as part of their existing letting business or ascertained any likely return on investment. They have not explored alternative locations on the estate. Their original plan to renovate the buildings has changed to demolition and rebuild. Their current letting business has occupancy rates of only 10% and expert evidence is that there is no obvious demand for tourist accommodation in the area.

[130] In each of Buckworth v Ross 1925 SLCR 94 sets out similar circumstances: there the resumption was refused. In Walker v McEwan 1946 SLCR 14 the resumption was refused as it would “have detrimental effects on the working and amenity of the holding” and the same is the case here. If, as is the case here, the proposed resumption will be in the interests of the general public as providing employment, Mackay’s Trustees v Colthart 1959 SLCR 43 is authority that evidence of urgent demand in the area for work of the nature contemplated must be offered up. No evidence was led as to the demand for employment in holiday lets in the area. Evidence would also have to be shown that the landlords had considered other areas less suitable for sheep. No evidence was led to show other areas had been considered.

[131] The application in Lord Brocket’s Trustees v Hodgeson 1961 SLCR 25 was refused as it would result in the creation of “an island” on the croft and no demand for additional council houses had been established. The landlords’ proposal here would create such an island and no evidence of additional short term holiday letting demand had been led.

[132] In Secretary of State for Air v Macdonald 1962 SLCR App 90 the application for resumption was refused on the basis that the landlords had other vacant land that could be used. This was raised by the crofter as an objection which the landlords in that case failed to answer. The same is the case here. Grimersta Estate Ltd v MacLeod 1972 SLCR (App) 128 held that the benefit in granting the resumption for a dwellinghouse was outweighed by the damage done to the croft. This is the case here.

[133] Shaw v Cummings 1987 SLCR 157 reiterates the approach in the foregoing four cases. Portman Trustees v Macrae 1971 SLT (Land Ct) 6 should be followed as preferring the crofter’s proposed development proposals to the landlords’ alternatives. The instant case is similar to Beardsall v Bell 1975 SLT (Land Ct) 2, Dunbeath Estate Ltd v Gunn (No 1) 1988 SLCR 52 and Fountain International Ltd v MacDonald 1991 SLCR 84: in those cases, resumption was refused where the land was important for sheltering stock.

[134] The court should consider the matters provided for section 20(1AC) of the 1993 Act. There is no decided case law on the matter but the matters apply here.

[135] The application is contrary to the Practice Note 1 as planning permission has not been applied for or granted. The suggestion that Practice Note 1 does not apply to this situation is incorrect. The overriding principle is that the court requires to be satisfied not only that the resumption is for a reasonable purpose in terms of section 20 but also that the purpose will actually be carried out. The examples given by Practice Note 1 are merely indicative of certain scenarios to assist applicants and do not detract from that principle.

[136] In the time since submitting their application to resume, the landlords have taken no steps to instruct architects or apply for full planning permission required for their proposed development. It is irrelevant whether the resumed land is for use by the landlords as opposed to being conveyed to the crofter or another third party. It is the landlords who must satisfy the court in all respects that the resumption should be granted (South Uist) Estates Limited v MacDonald 1983 SLCR 86).

[137] Whilst the court stated in Lands Improvement Holdings Landmatch SARL v Cole (Application RN SLC/39/14) that practice notes were for guidance and not law and could not import conditions as absolute requirements they did say that the practice note’s purpose was “to give guidance as to what the court looked for as evidence that the purpose for which resumption was sought was realistic, credible and feasible.” There would have to be circumstances to justify departure from a practice note. The landlords’ argument to justify departure, namely that Practice Note 1 “created a rule in addition to the legislation, especially where the circumstances are not apt for the Practice Note to be applied”, does not apply here. It is apt for Practice Note 1 to be applied because planning permission is required in this instance for the development proposed. The landlords have things the wrong way round in asking the court to grant resumption so that they could instruct an architect and apply for planning. This is on a par with the situation in Land Improvements.

[138] The court has no power to recall any order once made. It is imperative that resumption of croft land should not be lightly authorised for purposes which may soon fail (Secretary of State for Scotland v Shareholders of Lealt & Culnacnock Common Grazings 1982 SLT (Land Ct) 20). This is the case here. Land Improvement cites a number of other cases, all of which are authority that resumptions do not require proof of reasonable purpose in the abstract but require proof of a relevant purpose for which it is reasonable to grant in all the circumstances relevant to the interests specified in the statutory provisions.

[139] There is no basis to make any order conditional on planning permission such as is sometimes done in windfarm resumptions. In those cases they are supported by tenants and not conditional on finding a developer. Agreements are already in place subject to authorisation of resumption. Further, as the application is conjoined with the crofter’s application to purchase the court could not logically order the purchase of the croft subject to a resumption which might fail.

[140] All questions of expenses should be reserved pending the court’s decision and then addressed in the usual way with written submissions following thereon.

Discussion and decision

[141] There appears to be no dispute as between the parties on the relevant and applicable legal principles which were set out in and summarised by Lord McGhie in Nevis Estates Limited and others v Cameron 2011 SLCR 83 at paras [19] - [25] and which we have applied to the facts in hand. Nevis concerned competing applications to purchase and resume without necessarily imposing any strict order of priority. The statutory tests for each are not mirror images and there is a public interest consideration in any application to resume which arguably takes priority over a purchase application (Nevis, supra).

[142] The matters for determination are: (first) whether the landlords have made out a sufficient case in support of their application for resumption and (second) whether the landlords are able to satisfy the court that substantial hardship will be caused should the crofter’s application to purchase be successful. The evidence led by each side related to the various matters of potential relevance to each of the issues before us. In each application the onus lies on the landlords: in the case of the application for partial resumption, that the test in section 20(1) of the 1993 Act has been met so as to allow resumption and in the case of the purchase application, the landlords must satisfy us that the test in section 13(2) of the 1993 Act has been met (Macaskill v Basil Baird & Sons Ltd and Another (supra)). The crofter led evidence to counter the landlords’ case and to support their position in respect of the inclusion of the southern apportionment and, by consequence, Loch BB.

[143] We have set out our position in respect of the landlords’ application to resume first.

Application to resume

[144] The landlords’ proposals have evolved since the application for resumption was lodged with the court. The original proposal was redevelopment of the two buildings on the resumption area and the current proposal is the demolition of the two existing buildings and erection of two new buildings in their place. The stated purpose for the resumption is two‑fold: to make safe what the landlords consider to be derelict and unsafe buildings and to take an opportunity to expand their existing holiday lettings business with two additional properties. In doing so, their existing staff of two would be increased, thus offering local employment.

[145] The crofter set out a number of objections to the proposal. In summary these are that the resumption will take land and buildings presently used for croft purposes out of the croft, resident wildlife will be disturbed, historic buildings will be demolished and the crofter will be unable to implement his own, longer term plans for the buildings and croft.

[146] In deciding whether the landlords proposals are for a reasonable purpose we have considered the limbs of the test set out in section 20(1) of the 1993 Act based on the evidence placed before us, together with the case authorities cited by the parties in their submissions.

Good of the croft

[147] We took particular account of the evidence of the crofter and Dr Ross regarding the routine use of the buildings for shelter for the flock and for storing hay. This was supported by the evidence of Mr McGillivray, albeit Mr McGillivray had only visited last autumn. Mr Franklin had also observed use for storage though some time before. By Mrs Franklin’s own admission she had visited the buildings very infrequently and not gone inside. While Mr Oxley had not noted the buildings being used for storage or any vehicles his evidence was that he had visited the buildings for a specific reason (a possible hide) and, after no agreement was reached on this, had no reason to visit again. In our inspection we observed that the two buildings are derelict and in a poor state, however we did see that they were both being used to store small amounts of hay, presumably for supplementary feed.

[148] Notwithstanding the evidence of Mr Ross and Mr McGillivray, we saw no evidence of a fank or sheep handling in the area on the day of the inspection. It is level ground but appeared that it could hold water and we questioned if this was a good place to site a fank. We did not consider this to be a material point.

[149] The partial resumption area is surrounded by working croft land. Clearly, the use proposed by the landlords will result in additional visitors to the area, likely on a short term basis. The crofter and Dr Ross both expressed concerns around the potential impact on the land, the wildlife and the crofting business posed by short term visitors taking holiday lettings. We heard their concerns over the potential risks including security and biohazard concerns. It does not automatically follow that all visitors will behave in an irresponsible manner. However additional short term visitors must increase the risks of harm to amenity and security and the potential adverse impact on the croft when compared to maintaining the buildings for their current use or redevelopment for use by a family living and working there permanently.

[150] We take note of the position of the landlords that the crofter’s own plans for the renovation of the buildings are not advanced. This is the landlords’ application however and the onus is on the landlords to satisfy the court that the tests have been met with regard to their own plans (Macaskill v Basil Baird & Sons Ltd and Another (supra)). There is evidence that the crofter has made use of the buildings to support crofting on the land over the years. With regard to any plans for redevelopment on the crofter’s part, we consider it to be a reasonable position for the crofter to take that further investment will only be made after the crofter has acquired ownership of the land in question.

[151] Taking account of the evidence presented we do not consider that the landlords’ proposals will confer any good on the croft. The resumption will take land and buildings out of crofting tenure. The croft will lose access to and use of the two buildings and land. Loss of the buildings means loss of storage and shelter. The croft will lose the opportunity to develop the buildings for future use for renovation for a family. The nesting habitat of the owls will be lost. There will be an increased risk of disturbance to the land and stock by an increase in traffic and visitors. Two historical buildings will be demolished and replaced. This may or may not have an impact on the fledgling tour business but we consider it reasonable to assume that the visual impact of the historical buildings, even where dilapidated, is likely to be greater than bare land or new buildings. Income from that business is intended to supplement and be reinvested into the croft business for the good of the croft.

[152] The disadvantages are not outweighed by the potential opportunity to use the compensation paid for new facilities. Any new facilities will need a suitable alternative site to be identified and planning and technical consents to be obtained. Construction will need to take place. During that time the existing shelter and storage would be lost.

Good of the estate

[153] The landlords propose to demolish, rebuild and use the new buildings as holiday lettings to supplement their existing lettings business. No quotes or costings have been obtained for the proposed demolition and build works. By their own evidence the landlords have not considered any other sites within the estate. There is no defined nor ascertainable plan around delivery of the landlords’ proposals and no business plan has been prepared for the intended lettings, including any additional employees needed to assist.

[154] Despite Mrs Franklin’s view that there is some demand for tourism in the area, this was not the view of either expert. Ms Acheson expressed concerns around the viability of the estate achieving a return on the necessary capital expenditure. The evidence of the landlords is that the estate is already loss making. Even without the benefit of costings and a business plan, it is clear that the proposals would involve significant capital expenditure by the landlords - both for the required demolition as well as a rebuild - without any evidence of a viable resulting income stream in return.

[155] Taking all of the evidence into account we do not consider that the landlords have demonstrated that the resumption would be for the good of the estate.

Interests of the crofting community in the locality of the croft and the public interest

[156] While separate matters for consideration, they can be considered together with regard to the intention of the landlords to offer affordable holidays in the new properties. In doing so, the landlords would utilise local supplies and labour, both for the redevelopment works and the resulting business. The existing estate staff of two would be increased to service the additional lettings. The landlords’ proposals might be said to contribute to the public interest if the stated aim of offering reasonably priced holiday lettings is achieved and the demand for these is there. The new lettings could benefit the local community with increased economic activity from the tourists staying at the cottages. It is also reasonable to assume that awareness around crofting would be raised given that the lettings would be adjacent to the working croft.

[157] Such supply and employment prospects and resulting economic activity in the wider community are, however, entirely dependent on viable development proposals and a viable holiday letting business. We require to be confident that the stated purpose of the resumption is realisticand achievable (Secretary of State for Scotland v Shareholders of Lealt & Culnacnock Common Grazings (supra); Lands Improvement Holdings Landmatch SARL v Cole (supra)). We take account of the view of both experts that there is no obvious demand for tourism. Our concern is that the landlords’ plans would not in fact come to fruition as not being economically viable. No evidence was provided to support any urgent demand for employment in the area (similar to Mackay’s Trustees v Colthart 1959 SLCR 43). As such we find the proposals would not serve the interests of the community or public interest in this regard.

Public interest
